title: The Seven Sacraments and Holy Orders
author: Dn Yonnas
summary: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo teaching on the Sacrament of Holy Orders, set within the seven Mysteries by which invisible grace is given through visible signs. It defends the divine institution of an ordained ministry, sets out the three degrees of bishop, priest, and deacon by apostolic succession, and describes the manner, conditions, and obligations of ordination.

sections.p: In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a Mystery or Sacrament is a sacred sign instituted by Christ through which invisible grace is given by means of a visible sign. The Church confesses seven such Mysteries: Baptism, Confirmation (the seal of the Holy Spirit), the Holy Eucharist, Penance (Repentance and Confession), Unction of the Sick, Matrimony, and Holy Orders. In each Mystery the Church looks for three things together: the divine institution by which Christ established it, the visible sign through which it is administered, and the invisible grace which the Holy Spirit grants through that sign.

Holy Orders holds a special place among the Mysteries, for it is the Mystery through which the clergy are ordained, and it is by means of the ordained ministry that the other Mysteries are celebrated and handed on. The parish treatise summarized here is devoted especially to this Sacrament of the priesthood.

sections.h2: The Sacrament of Holy Orders: Definition

sections.p: Holy Orders is the Sacrament through which the clergy are ordained to celebrate the various services of the Church. Some who reject this teaching claim that Christ did not distinguish anyone in His Church, that all members are the same, and that there is no need to set apart special persons as ministers. The source firmly rejects this view, showing from Scripture and history that Christ Himself established an ordered ministry distinct from the body of the faithful.

sections.h3: Why an Ordained Ministry Is Necessary

sections.p: The treatise gives a series of reasons drawn from the New Testament and from the witness of history. Together they show that Christ deliberately set apart certain persons, gave them powers not given to all, and provided that this ministry should continue after Him.

list: Christ set apart special persons as Apostles, spending a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12-13).
He gave them special privileges not given to others, such as the power to bind and to loose (Matthew 18:18).
Sending them out before His ascension, He promised to be with them 'even unto the end of the world,' a promise understood to extend to their successors also (Matthew 28:20).
When Judas fell away, the Apostles gathered, prayed, and chose another to fill his place, showing the office had to be preserved (Acts 1:15-26).
The clergy had duties the laity could not perform; the deacon Philip preached in Samaria but could not lay on hands to give the Holy Spirit, so Peter and John were sent to do so (Acts 8:14-17).
Scripture lays down distinct conditions for choosing bishops and deacons (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).
Scripture appoints a definite procedure for ordination, namely the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14).
All historians agree that ministers have existed in the Church since the first century, and the ancient churches keep lists of their bishops from the beginning.

sections.p: This Sacrament was instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. It was He who appointed the twelve Apostles and the seventy disciples, and He who sent the Apostles into the world before His ascension to teach and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, promising to be with them always. Saint Paul teaches that it was Christ Himself who appointed some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers.

sections.quote: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost ... and lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.

sections.p: Addressing the ministers of the Church of Ephesus, Paul warned them to take heed to themselves and to all the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made them overseers. According to the power given them by the Lord, the Apostles in turn appointed bishops, priests, and deacons in the churches they established, so that the ministry was handed on in unbroken succession.

sections.h2: The Visible Sign and the Invisible Grace

sections.p: Holy Orders, like every Mystery, has its outward sign and its inward gift. The treatise identifies two visible signs: the laying on of hands, attested in Scripture for bishops, priests, and deacons; and the prayers of consecration that accompany it.

list: The laying on of hands: for bishops (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6), priests (1 Timothy 5:22), and deacons (Acts 6:6).
The prayers of consecration (Acts 6:6; 14:23).

sections.p: The invisible grace is a divine gift suited to the service to which the minister is called. Paul reminds Timothy not to neglect the gift given him by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery, and to stir up the gift of God given by the laying on of Paul's own hands. This gift is bestowed by the Holy Spirit, who alone can enable the minister to perform his duties.

sections.quote: Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.

sections.h2: The Three Degrees of Holy Orders

sections.p: The Bible mentions three degrees of the ordained ministry: the bishop, the priest, and the deacon. Each degree has its own God-given duties, which cannot be performed by a lower order.

This is the highest degree, for which Scripture gives detailed conditions (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1). The Apostles consecrated bishops, ordained priests, and ordained deacons, and the bishops whom the Apostles consecrated received that same right of ordination. To Titus, Paul wrote that he had left him in Crete to set things in order and to ordain priests in every city; to Timothy he warned, 'Lay hands suddenly on no man.'

list: Ordination of the clergy.
Trial of the clergy and rebuking them: 'Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses' (1 Timothy 5:19-20).
Consecration of the Holy Oil used for the Sacrament of Confirmation.
Consecration of the altar and the Holy vessels for a new church or new vessels.
The right to celebrate all the Church's sacraments and rites.
Management of the general affairs of the Church.

sections.p: Priests (called 'elders' in many translations) are mentioned throughout the New Testament. The Apostles ordained elders in every church, and those who rule well are to be counted worthy of double honor. The sick are to call for the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. The priest has the right to celebrate the Mysteries entrusted to him and all the rites of the Church, and the right to teach and to preach.

sections.quote: Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.

sections.p: Deacons are mentioned in Acts 6:3-6, Philippians 1:1, and 1 Timothy 3. A deacon does not have the right to celebrate any of the Mysteries, but only to help the priest and the bishop in celebrating them, to keep good order in the church, to read the appointed portions of Scripture, to teach and preach, and to perform any service the bishop or priest may ask of him. The Orders of the Apostles call the deacon 'the bishop's eyes and ears.'

The treatise also recalls the former degree of deaconess, whose function was to serve the women of the Church, to keep good order in the place set apart for them, and to anoint the bodies of women at Confirmation after the priest had anointed only their foreheads. The Didascalia provided that no woman should approach the bishop except in the company of a deaconess, and that a deaconess, not a deacon, should be sent to women's houses. This order appears to have existed in apostolic times: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant (or deaconess) of the church at Cenchreae, and his instruction to enroll certain widows is thought by some to refer to the list of deaconesses.

list: A bishop is consecrated by the laying on of the hands of at least three bishops, for one bishop alone cannot consecrate a bishop.
A priest or a deacon is ordained by the laying on of the hands of a single bishop.

Ordination is never repeated for the same degree if the person was previously ordained in a lawful way; the Apostolic Canons (68) hold that re-ordination renders both the ordained and the ordainer worthy of excommunication.

No money may be paid for any ordination; when Simon offered money for God's gift, Peter rebuked him, 'Thy money perish with thee' (Acts 8:18-20). Any ordination performed for payment is unlawful, and the bishop who accepts money should be excommunicated.
They must be sure that the call comes from God, for 'no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron' (Hebrews 5:4).
They must be blameless, good examples to the congregation in word, conduct, charity, spirit, faith, and purity (1 Timothy 4:12; cf. 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).
They must be well acquainted with the Bible and the teachings of the Church.

sections.p: They must not serve as hired men working merely for wages, but as good shepherds who feed the flock of God willingly, not for filthy lucre, knowing the sheep are theirs and that they are responsible to keep them from the beasts and to feed them. The hireling flees when the wolf comes, but the good shepherd is ready to offer any sacrifice needed for the sake of the sheep, after the pattern of the Lord.

sections.quote: The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

sections.p: Holy Orders, divinely instituted by Christ and handed on through the laying on of hands in apostolic succession, secures for the Church its bishops, priests, and deacons, through whom the other Mysteries are celebrated and the faithful are fed. The ordained minister receives a real and invisible grace of the Holy Spirit through the visible sign, and is bound both before and after ordination to a life of holiness and faithful shepherding, that he may serve not as a hireling but as a true shepherd of the flock of God.
